newsitem.title: USA: White House says tobacco deal not tough enough.
newsitem.headline: White House says tobacco deal not tough enough.

text.p: An adviser to President Bill Clinton said on Monday the $368.5 billion tobacco deal between states and the tobacco industry needs to be toughened to include stiffer penalties against tobacco companies.
The White House also wants greater power given to the Food and Drug Administration to regulate tobacco as a drug, said Bruce Reed, domestic policy adviser to the president.
"It needs to be strengthened in some key ways," he told NBC's "Today" programme. "We need to make sure that we give the FDA the full authority it needs to do its job."
Giving the FDA that power, Reed said, was "central to our ability to reduce smoking and reduce nicotine addiction over time."

He said one problem the White House had with the current proposal, which calls for the tobacco companies to pay states more than $368.5 billion over 25 years, was that it did not go far enough in penalising tobacco companies if they fail to reduce the number of teens who smoke.
"The agreement calls for financial penalties if the company comes up short in reducing teen smoking," Reed said.

"We think they need to be strengthened. There's some question as to whether those penalties should be tax deductible as they are in the proposed settlement but we think we can come up with a very tough agreement."

He told NBC the White House was currently talking to public health experts to make recommendations to the president. He said Clinton would then review the proposal and make a statement on it within "the next month or so."
